brief.scenario: Ms Rachel Linford, 42, has an 18 mm invasive breast cancer (no special type, grade 2, ER positive, HER2 negative) in her left breast. It is palpable, and axillary ultrasound is normal. After the MDT and a discussion with her consultant, she has chosen wide local excision with sentinel lymph node biopsy, followed by radiotherapy. The consultant has asked you to discuss the operation with her.
brief.task: Discuss the proposed operation with Ms Linford and seek her consent. A consent form is available.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: What she knows and wants, the operation, what may follow, alternatives, risks that matter to her, her decision.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Reading generic risks and skipping the chance of a second operation.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "What do you understand about the operation, and what matters most to you?"

grid.label: Understanding and priorities
grid.fail: Starts reading risks without asking what she knows.
grid.pass: Introduces self, confirms identity, asks what she understands about the diagnosis and plan.
grid.high: Asks what matters most to her about the operation and uses it to shape the discussion.

grid.label: Explaining the operation
grid.fail: Cannot explain what wide local excision or sentinel node biopsy involve.
grid.pass: Removes the lump with a rim of healthy tissue, and the first lymph node(s) draining the breast, under general anaesthetic.
grid.high: Explains the node is found with a radioactive tracer injected beforehand and blue dye in theatre.

grid.label: Possible further surgery
grid.fail: Does not mention that a second operation may be needed.
grid.pass: Warns that cancer at the edge of the tissue removed means further surgery; about 1 in 5 women need another operation.
grid.high: Adds that a sentinel node containing cancer usually means further armpit treatment: surgery or radiotherapy.

grid.label: Alternatives
grid.fail: Presents the operation as the only option.
grid.pass: Mastectomy is an alternative with the same survival; no operation is also her choice. Conservation needs radiotherapy.
grid.high: Mentions reconstruction with mastectomy and checks she is still happy with her choice.

grid.label: Material risks
grid.fail: Lists only bleeding, infection and a scar.
grid.pass: Bleeding, infection, fluid collection, change in breast shape; blue urine and skin staining; numbness and arm swelling.
grid.high: Gives figures: arm swelling about 5 in 100 and numbness about 11 in 100 at a year; rare dye allergy.

grid.label: Understanding and voluntary decision
grid.fail: Pushes for a signature today without checking understanding.
grid.pass: Asks her to explain back; confirms the decision is hers and she can change her mind.
grid.high: Offers more time, or a further talk with the consultant, before she signs.

grid.label: Form, record and next steps
grid.fail: Treats the signature as the consent.
grid.pass: Completes the form with her, gives a copy, records the discussion in the notes.
grid.high: Explains pre-assessment, written lymphoedema advice, and that the consultant will see her on the day.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Hi, I'm here to do your consent form for the lumpectomy.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: Ms Linford: “What exactly will you do?”

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Take the lump out and some glands. Standard stuff.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Not really, this is what the MDT decided.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Risks are bleeding, infection and a scar. Sign here and here.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: Ms Linford: “Can I think about it?”

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: It's best we get it done today, the list is next week. That's you consented.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Hello, I'm Dr Patel, one of the surgical doctors. Can I check your name and date of birth? What do you understand about the operation?

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Ms Linford: “You're taking the lump out and checking a gland.”

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: That's right. Under a general anaesthetic, we remove the lump with a rim of healthy tissue, and the first lymph node or nodes that drain the breast.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: If the cancer reaches the edge of what we remove, you'd need further surgery; about 1 in 5 women do.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: The alternative is removing the whole breast, with the same survival. Not operating is also your choice. Keeping the breast means radiotherapy afterwards.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Risks: bleeding, infection, fluid collecting, a change in breast shape. The dye turns urine blue and can stain the skin. The arm can feel numb or swell.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Can you tell me in your own words what we'll do and what could happen? It's your decision, and you can change your mind.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I'll fill in the form with you, give you a copy, and write our discussion in your notes.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Hello, I'm Dr Patel, one of the surgical doctors. Can I check your name and date of birth? What do you understand about the operation, and what matters most to you?

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Ms Linford: “Keeping my breast. And I really don't want a second operation.”

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Thanks, that helps. Under a general anaesthetic we remove the lump with a rim of healthy tissue. Before surgery a small radioactive injection, then blue dye in theatre, show us the first lymph nodes draining the breast, and we remove those.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Since a second operation matters to you: about 1 in 5 women need one, because cancer reaches the edge of the tissue. If the node contains cancer, you'd usually need further treatment to the armpit, surgery or radiotherapy.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Ms Linford: “Would a mastectomy avoid that?”

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: It lowers the chance of more breast surgery, but survival is the same, it's a bigger operation, and you might want a reconstruction. Not operating is also your choice. Are you still happy keeping the breast, with radiotherapy afterwards?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Risks: bleeding, infection, fluid, a change in shape. The dye turns urine blue and can stain the skin; allergy is rare. At a year, about 5 in 100 women have arm swelling and 11 in 100 numbness.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Can you tell me what you're agreeing to? You don't have to sign today; you can talk to your consultant again.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: If you're ready, we'll complete the form together; you'll get a copy. Then pre-assessment, written advice on arm swelling, and your consultant sees you on the day.

failures.move: Not mentioning that 1 in 5 women need a second operation.
failures.consequence: A material risk, especially to her; a re-excision then comes as a shock and damages trust.
The MDT recommends; she decides. Mastectomy and no operation are reasonable alternatives she must hear.
Omits lymphoedema, numbness and dye effects, the risks a reasonable woman in her position would want to know.
Consent under pressure, without checked understanding, is not valid consent.

recovery.line: One important thing I should add: about 1 in 5 women need a further operation.
There are also risks specific to the lymph node surgery.
You don't need to sign today.

knowledge.fact: Consent: options including no treatment, material risks judged from her position, checked understanding, time, and a record. The form is not the consent.
Radial margin with tumour on ink (0 mm): offer further surgery; invasive cancer within 1 mm: consider it.
About 1 in 5 women in England have a reoperation after breast-conserving surgery.
Sentinel node macrometastasis: further axillary surgery or radiotherapy. Micrometastases only: none.
After sentinel node biopsy at 12 months: lymphoedema 5%, sensory loss 11%.

recall.think: Which risks would matter to her?
recall.say: "You could choose a mastectomy, or no operation. Let me explain."

numbers.meaning: arm swelling a year after sentinel node biopsy

partner.opening: Ms Linford has come to clinic to discuss her operation. Please begin when you're ready.
partner.actorBrief: You are Rachel Linford, 42, a primary school teacher with two children aged 8 and 11. You were told of your left breast cancer two weeks ago and chose to keep your breast after seeing your consultant. You are calm but anxious. Your main worry: needing a second operation, because of time off work and the children. Say so if asked what matters to you. If the candidate mentions reoperation, ask: "Would a mastectomy avoid that?" If given balanced information, stay with breast conservation. If risks are listed without explanation, ask: "What does the dye do?" If pressed to sign, say: "Can I think about it?" If asked to explain back, give a fair summary.

reveals.trigger: Asks what matters most to her
reveals.finding: "Keeping my breast. And not needing a second operation."
"Is the radioactive injection safe?" (a small dose, given before surgery).
"Does that mean I can't have blood taken from that arm?"
"Lump and the first glands out; maybe another operation; the arm could swell; my choice."

push.question: Would a mastectomy avoid a second operation?
push.expect: It lowers the chance of further breast surgery but not axillary treatment; same survival; bigger operation; her choice.

push.question: Do I have to sign today?
push.expect: No; she can take time and change her mind until the operation.

curveballs.prompt: "Can I have blood tests and blood pressure on that arm afterwards?"
curveballs.safeAnswer: No consistent evidence these increase lymphoedema; a shared decision, with written advice on reducing risk.

curveballs.prompt: "What if the node has cancer in it?"
curveballs.safeAnswer: Macrometastasis: usually further axillary surgery or radiotherapy, decided at MDT; micrometastases only: no further axillary treatment.
Answer honestly: the consultant's team operates; she can ask who will, and the consultant will see her on the day.
